meta.panelHeading: Step by Step numbers in a group of 100 women
meta.tableCaption: Women at each stage of the protection order process

steps.head: Every one of these women had grounds to apply for a protection order
steps.body: All had been beaten, strangled, raped, threatened with a weapon or stalked by a partner in the past year.

steps.head: 77 did not
steps.body: Only about a fifth of women who could have applied actually did. The researchers say that although this share may not hold for the country as a whole, it points one way: most women who may benefit from a protection order never start the process.

steps.head: 2 who started the process did not complete the form
steps.body: The research found that some women were talked out of lodging an application by police officers or court officials. Others did not have any help in filling in the form — which must be in English. Some took the papers home, where their partner found them and tore them up.

steps.of: women were granted a temporary protection order
steps.head: 2 women's applications were not successful
steps.body: A protection order comes into effect only once the man — called the respondent — has had it handed to him. Some men could not be found, some had left the area, and some were already in custody for another offence, where officials sometimes wrongly said they could not be served.

steps.of: women went on to make the temporary protection order permanent
steps.head: 7 women decided no to go ahead
steps.body: The most common reason why women decided not to go ahead with making the order permanent was that family — either hers or his — begged her not to go through with it, apologising and promising that he would change. Others feared that getting a permanent order would make the violence worse. However, even with a temporary order, women were protected for several weeks.

steps.of: was granted a final protection order, with no expiry date
steps.head: Only 1 of the 12 women who applied for the permanent order did not get it
steps.body: Almost all women who applied to have the temporary order made permanent were successful. Of the group of 100 we started with, 11 get to this point. But the justice system reached 19 women in total, each who had protection for some time, even if the order didn't become permanent.
